source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Mapping of 65 articles (1990-2016) covering 37 biases. Anchoring (26 articles), confirmation (23) and overconfidence/optimism are the most studied. Almost no tested fixes.
numbers: 65 articles, 37 biases. Debiasing work covers only 6 of 37 biases.
quote: none of the primary studies provide strong empirical evidence for the effectiveness of debiasing techniques
limits: Mapping study, not a meta-analysis: no pooled effect sizes.
agent_relevance: The field has a long list of named biases but almost no tested mitigations. Do not assume a named fix works for the agent without testing it.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Confirmation bias shows up in testing as positive test bias: developers test with data that fits how the program is meant to work. Specification completeness, domain knowledge and presence of errors moderate it. Programming expertise seems to have no effect.
numbers: Primary study P31 (Leventhal/Teasley line); the review gives direction only, no effect sizes.
limits: Second-hand summary of older studies, which used small samples and mostly students.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G3: a checker that only runs the cases the fix was built for will pass wrong answers. Experience does not remove the habit, so the guardrail must be structural.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Review says people trained in logical reasoning and hypothesis testing showed less confirmation bias in testing (study P4, Calikli and Bener). It also says experienced but no-longer-active developer/testers showed less bias than experienced active ones.
numbers: Based on one primary study (P4).
limits: This is a correlation between skill and bias, not a training experiment. The word 'trained' in the review is stronger than the data (see b05).
agent_relevance: The 'logic training reduced confirmation bias' claim is weak. Treat it as a hint that falsification skill predicts less bias, not proof that teaching it fixes it.

source: Mohanani, Salman, Turhan, Rodriguez, Ralph (2020) Cognitive Biases in Software Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
finding: Proposed fixes for confirmation bias: ask testers to seek evidence of problems, not evidence it works (P32); generate and compare several design options at once (P37). For anchoring: planning poker, multiple design candidates, directed questions, awareness. The review labels all of these untested suggestions.
numbers: Fixes listed in the review's Table 10; none with an effect size.
limits: Review itself says research on group estimation from multiple anchors is mixed and that raising awareness alone is unlikely to help.
agent_relevance: Matches our S4 and S5 design: ask the agent to try to break the answer, and use several candidates. Each still needs its own measurement on the agent.

source: Calikli, Arslan, Bener (2010) Confirmation Bias in Software Development and Testing: Effects of Company Size, Experience and Reasoning Skills (PPIG)
finding: Wason selection task and rule-discovery task given to developers and testers. Years of development or testing experience did not predict hypothesis-testing skill or test severity. Abstract reasoning did: graduate students beat company staff.
numbers: N=88 (large telecom 34, small firms 8+12, grad students 28). Experience vs test severity: n=27 testers and n=50 developers, no significant correlation. Abstract questions, students vs staff: chi2(1)=8.114, p<.005; software-themed: chi2(1)=7.085, p<.01. Large vs small company eliminative index z=-3.82, p<.001.
quote: regardless of experience and company size, abilities such as logical reasoning and strategic hypothesis testing
limits: Correlational, small, mixed groups tested under different conditions (authors note release-rush stress for staff). Not a training experiment.
agent_relevance: Skill, not seniority, predicts falsifying behaviour. For the agent: do not rely on a 'senior expert' persona to cure confirmation; install the falsification step itself.

source: Calikli, Arslan, Bener (2010) PPIG
finding: The link from confirmation bias to defects is thin. Only 5 developers had usable churn data. The one developer who abandoned the interactive test had the highest defect ratio (0.86). Testers with fewer falsifying tendencies produced production defects above average, but the authors also say low-bias testers reported more bugs and still overlooked many.
numbers: 5 developers, defect ratios 0.86, 0.38, 0.20, 0.00, 0.11. Spearman 0.8234 between reported bugs and production defects among testers.
limits: Five data points; reported-bug count and severity confounded; authors list threats themselves. Weakest link in the 'bias causes defects' chain.
agent_relevance: Do not cite this as proof that confirmation bias causes defects. Use it only as motivation.

source: Shepperd, Mair, Jorgensen (2018) An Experimental Evaluation of a De-biasing Intervention for Professional Software Developers
finding: A random high or low productivity anchor shifted professionals' estimates of their own productivity strongly. A short workshop on judgement biases cut the anchor effect but did not remove it, mostly for the high anchor, and cut variance threefold.
numbers: 410 developers in company settings (292 in the earlier no-workshop series). Anchor effect robust Cohen's d=1.19 (trimmed mean gap 60.5, 95% CI 51.6-69.4, about 350%). With workshop d=0.72.
limits: Workshop and no-workshop groups come from different series and countries (not randomised); analysis dropped UK, Nepal, Vietnam leaving 272 participants. Own-project productivity, not code tasks.
agent_relevance: Awareness training helps but leaves a big residue. Telling the agent 'beware anchoring' should be expected to shrink, not remove, the effect; measure it.

source: Gren and Svensson (2021) Is it Possible to Disregard Obsolete Requirements? A Family of Experiments in Software Effort Estimation
finding: Six experiments. Requirements explicitly marked as not-to-be-implemented still raised effort estimates in every experiment: an anchoring-and-adjustment effect that survives an instruction to ignore. Over-estimation was around twice the share of obsolete items, with wide intervals.
numbers: N=461 (students and practitioners), Bayesian analysis. Effect sizes 0.54, 0.75, 0.54 across the three experiment sets. Experiment 4 (industry) group means 4.62, 6.69, 8.33 for none, some, more obsolete items; R2=0.527. Smaller effect in the field setting than with students.
limits: Authors say the effect may exist mainly where an outsider who will not implement the work estimates. Earlier single studies had about 20 participants each.
agent_relevance: An instruction to 'ignore this' does not cancel irrelevant context. For the agent: strip dropped candidates and stale text out of the working context rather than telling it to disregard them.

source: Wyrich, Merz, Graziotin (2022) Anchoring Code Understandability Evaluations Through Task Descriptions
finding: A one-sentence hint in the task description (code is hard or easy) shifted self-rated code comprehensibility. Professionals were anchored as much as students. It extends and replicates an earlier student-only experiment.
numbers: N=256 (50 professionals, 206 students), randomised three groups. Scenario to rating path coefficient 0.165, p<.001, 95% CI [0.071, 0.265]; code difficulty itself 0.418; R2=0.223. Role effect 0.033 (n.s.). Earlier student-only study: d=-1.29.
limits: Subjective rating only, not performance. The scenario effect is smaller than the effect of true difficulty.
agent_relevance: Task framing words change self-assessment even for experts. Prompts that say 'this is easy' may bias the agent's own confidence ratings.

source: Wyrich, Preikschat, Graziotin, Wagner (2021) The Mind Is a Powerful Place: How Showing Code Comprehensibility Metrics Influences Code Understanding
finding: A displayed (made-up) comprehensibility metric value (4 or 8) anchored developers' ratings strongly but did not change time or correctness on comprehension questions. The rating moved, the work did not.
numbers: N=43 students (20 easy group, 23 hard group). Rating difference d=-1.29, 95% CI of mean diff [-8.02, -2.83]; effect on timed actual understanding d=-0.006, p=.5385.
limits: Small student sample; double-blind but one setting.
agent_relevance: Anchoring can hit the report of confidence while leaving the work untouched. Judge the agent on outcomes, not on its stated confidence.

source: Gren and Svensson (2021) Obsolete requirements family of experiments: replication structure
finding: Replication note: Experiments 1 and 2 re-ran the original (Experiment 0) with the same setup; Experiment 3 doubled the spec size and obsolete items; Experiment 4 moved to industry; 5 and 6 used the teams' own requirements. The effect appeared every time, but smaller in industry.
numbers: Effect sizes 0.54, 0.75, 0.54 (not averaged by authors).
limits: Field data thin; authors warn against averaging across sets analysed separately.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: ownership of the outcome shrinks anchoring. An agent that must run its own answer may anchor less than one that only comments.

source: Jones and Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases (NeurIPS)
finding: Anchoring test on code models Codex and CodeGen: prepend a buggy function that nearly solves a HumanEval prompt. Accuracy falls and the output copies parts of the anchor, even when the anchor is not copied whole.
numbers: Codex produces the anchor's loop 'for var in' in 32%-61% of solutions and 'print(var)' in 26%-44%; inside correct solutions the loop still appears 3%-11%. Add-var anchor: 'return tmp' in 26%-46% (Codex), 13%-79% (CodeGen); verbatim copy only 7%-12% (Codex), 4%-12% (CodeGen). Accuracy lower than the no-anchor baseline at every anchor size.
limits: Old models (Codex, CodeGen), HumanEval only; no instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Earlier wrong attempts left in the context act as anchors. Supports dropping failed candidates from context before retry (S5), not just labelling them wrong.

source: Malberg, Poletukhin, Schuster, Groh (2025) A Comprehensive Evaluation of Cognitive Biases in LLMs
finding: 30 biases across 20 LLMs in managerial decision scenarios, 30,000 tests. All 30 appear in at least some models. Anchoring is strong on average, confirmation bias weaker, availability weak.
numbers: Mean bias score across 20 models (random baseline about 0): anchoring 0.39, confirmation bias 0.15, availability heuristic 0.11, framing 0.41, information bias 0.54. Per-model anchoring ranges from -0.05 to 0.67; confirmation from -0.18 to 0.72.
limits: Managerial text vignettes, discrete choices, not code.
agent_relevance: Anchoring is the bias to expect and guard; confirmation varies hugely by model, so test the chosen model.

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: 13,465-prompt dataset on admissions-style decisions. Compares awareness prompts, contrastive examples, counterfactual prompts and a self-help method where the model rewrites its own prompt. Self-help works best; some other mitigations cause failure cases.
numbers: GPT-4 framing: admits 40.5% more students under a frame. Self-help leaves 0% to 2.7% biased prompt elements in GPT-4 and 0% to 6% in Llama 2 (framing, status quo, group attribution).
limits: 2023-era models only (GPT-4, Llama 2); admission and hiring vignettes; contrastive prompts sometimes produced one-option answers.
agent_relevance: A model rewriting the problem statement to remove biased cues is cheaper than hand-writing examples. Candidate for the S0/S1 reframing step.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in LLMs
finding: More thinking tokens do not cut bias. Reasoning models are not less biased than their non-reasoning siblings. Of six biases only anchoring appears in the human direction; the others lean the opposite way. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor lowered anchoring on all five items.
numbers: 30 vignettes, 7 models, 4 families, 12,350 calls, thinking ceilings 0/1k/4k/8k. Reasoning minus non-reasoning bias magnitude +0.031, t(29)=1.45, p=.157, dz=0.27. Anchoring d=1.89 (t(4)=5.02, pHolm=.037). Restating anchors: pooled shift -0.015, 95% CI [-0.026,-0.004], item-level t(4)=-2.65, p=.057 (five items).
limits: Five items per bias, so per-bias tests are weak; the restating effect is directional, not established. Requested thinking ceilings often not honoured (79% of DeepSeek-R1 calls exceeded the 1,024 ceiling).
agent_relevance: Thinking longer is not a bias remedy: keep the structural checks (G3) rather than relying on more reasoning. Restating the given numbers is a cheap probe to trial.

source: Kraishan (2026) Long Road to the Same Answer: confirmation and availability results
finding: Confirmation bias and availability do not appear in the human direction in the tested models: confirmation leans opposite in all seven models; availability is absent or negative.
numbers: Item-level tests with five items per bias; reversal reliable for framing, directional for escalation, confirmation and loss aversion.
limits: Vignette-based; five items per bias; the author calls most of it directional.
agent_relevance: G3 should not assume the model has a human-style confirmation bias on its own thoughts. The gain from G3 comes from checking unfitted cases, not from debiasing.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering (PROBE-SWE)
finding: Benchmark of paired biased and unbiased software engineering dilemmas for 8 biases (anchoring, availability, bandwagon, confirmation, framing, hindsight, hyperbolic discounting, overconfidence). Common prompting fixes did not significantly reduce per-bias sensitivity.
numbers: Median bias sensitivity: no strategy 12.9%; zero-shot chain-of-thought 16.1% (worse); implication prompting 13.3%; impersonated self-debiasing 10.2%; bias warning 10.3%; both together 8.3%. Seven small or mid models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1 mini/nano, Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1 distill).
limits: Cheap models, multiple-choice dilemmas; authors say frontier models were not tested. Bias sensitivity rises with complexity: high tier 17.0% vs low 8.1%.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought made SE bias worse. Warning-style debiasing helps only slightly. Do not count on a 'be careful' line as a guard.

source: Sovrano, Dominici, Bacchelli (2026) PROBE-SWE: axiomatic cues
finding: Axiomatic cue method: have the model first write out the best-practice rules (Prolog-style axioms) the dilemma depends on, then answer. Overall bias sensitivity fell about 51% on average (p<.001), apart from hindsight bias.
numbers: Best combined variants 6.3% to 7.5% versus 12.9% control; low tier 8.1% to 3.5%; high tier 17.0% to 12.2%. Open-ended version: gpt-4o-mini down 12.5 points (31% relative); llama-3.1-8b down 10.0 points (25%); bootstrap CIs wide ([-10.0, 35.0] and [-7.5, 27.5] points, 40 dilemmas).
limits: Not significant for every single model (gpt-4.1-nano and llama-3.1-8b in some cuts); hindsight bias not helped; open-ended sample only 40.
agent_relevance: Strongest tested LLM fix in SE: make hidden background rules explicit before answering. Consistent with G3: state what a good check must cover, then test against it.

source: Zhou, Saghi, Sabouri, Pandita, McGuire, Chattopadhyay (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development (ICSE)
finding: Observation of developers working with LLMs: about half of all actions were biased, more so when interacting with the LLM. Fixation-type biases led to the most reversed actions. Developers anchored on first solutions despite contradicting output.
numbers: 14 developers observed, 2,013 actions; 983 (48.8%) linked to bias. LLM actions 808 (40.2%); 456 (56.4%) of those biased; reversal rate 29.5% (238/808) for LLM actions. Fixation: 43.4% of cases reversed. Survey n=22 more.
limits: Small convenience sample, human coding of bias; students and professionals mixed; taxonomy built with one psychologist.
agent_relevance: Humans who check LLM output also anchor. The agent's own verifier should not share the producer's context where possible (independence).

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Cognitive Biases in LLM-Assisted Software Development: mitigation side
finding: Survey respondents proposed practices (test-first development, treating the AI as a tool, self-review). Respondents split on whether some biases mattered.
numbers: Survey n=22; for most categories at least 50% said the bias occurs often or always.
limits: Self-report; no test of whether the mitigations work.
agent_relevance: Test-driven development is the human-side analogue of G3.

source: Tommasel and Schedl (2026) Measuring Human-Like Bias in LLMs? A Critique of Human-Derived Bias Constructs in LLM Evaluation
finding: Argues that applying anchoring, framing and confirmation-bias tests to LLMs has an inferential gap from construct, subject and context mismatches. A model shifting with a prompt number does not show a human-like bias, and instruction tuning shapes answers to look normative.
numbers: Critique paper, no new experiments; proposes an analytical framework linking evidence type to warranted claims.
limits: Position paper; no counts.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for all LLM bias results here: they are prompt sensitivity. For our agent that is enough, because the guardrail only needs the behaviour reduced.

source: Malberg et al. (2025) heatmap: per-model range
finding: Per-model spread is large. The smallest Llama (1B) looks unbiased because it fails to decide in 33% of tests. Only status-quo and disposition effect showed strong negative direction on average.
numbers: Anchoring column spans -0.05 to 0.67 across 20 models; confirmation -0.18 to 0.72; random baseline about 0.
limits: Authors caution that low bias can reflect failure to follow the task.
agent_relevance: A low bias score is not good reasoning. Measure bias and task accuracy together.

source: Mohanani et al. (2020) mapping study, Section 4.4
finding: Review warns that fixes such as keeping detailed records of past experience may fail because documents get long and out of date, and that model-based forecasting avoids anchoring but needs data projects lack.
numbers: Qualitative; 65 articles.
limits: Reviewers' judgement, not data.
agent_relevance: Cheap structural fixes (code checks) beat 'keep notes' fixes; agrees with the Schema rule of keeping checks in code.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task; Klayman and Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information
finding: Not opened this session; known via Calikli and Mohanani. Wason's 2-4-6 task: most people test only triples that fit their rule. Klayman and Ha later argued this positive test strategy is not always an error: it is fine when the true rule is narrow.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Recorded from memory and from the Calikli paper's description; not verified.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for G3: positive tests are fine when the hypothesis is rarer than the data; they fail when the true rule is broader, as with ARC fits that match every example.

source: Leventhal, Teasley, Rohlman (1994) Analyses of factors related to positive test bias in software testing
finding: Not opened this session; named in Mohanani's review (P31). Described there: specification completeness and domain knowledge moderate positive test bias, and programming expertise has no effect.
numbers: Numbers not read.
limits: Cited second-hand only.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that spec completeness, not seniority, lowers positive test bias.

source: Aranda and Easterbrook (2005) Anchoring and adjustment in software estimation (ESEC/FSE)
finding: Not opened. Gren and Svensson cite it as a case where anchoring in software estimation was not explained by the subjects' experience of cost estimation.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Second-hand, from the Gren and Svensson introduction.
agent_relevance: Another sign that numeric context moves estimates regardless of experience.
